passage: From behind the shop counter, Tejas watched his son Hrithik: twenty-five, back in their small town for the third time in two years, this time after leaving a call-centre job in Pune. At that age Tejas had been married, running this hardware shop and paying off the loan. The neighbours had started asking. At dinner he nearly said, "When will you settle?" He had said it before, and it had ended with a slammed door. Instead he tore a roti and asked, "What did you like in Pune, and what did you hate?" Hrithik looked up, surprised. "Liked the training part. Hated the night shifts." "Hmm. And next?" "Maybe teaching computers. I'm checking the institute in town." Tejas nodded slowly. It wasn't the life he'd had. Maybe it didn't need to be.

qa.a: A call-centre job.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about as he watched Hrithik?
qa.a: He worried Hrithik wasn't settling, since at that age Tejas had been married and running the shop, and the neighbours were asking.

qa.q: Why did asking what he liked and hated work better than "When will you settle?"
qa.a: It invited Hrithik to share instead of defend himself, which avoided another slammed door and brought out his plan to teach computers.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when his father asks a question instead of passing a verdict?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and respected, and more willing to talk about what comes next.

passage: In the queue at the district records office, Ganga watched her son Farhan fill in the form for his transcript. Twenty-five, still in his old room at home, now leaving his second job to study animation. Her sister had said on the phone, "He's drifting, Ganga. Put your foot down." The words had sat in her chest all week. But here Farhan was, checking every box twice, chatting politely with the clerk, fixing a wrong date without fuss. She realised she had never asked him what the course actually involved. On the bus home, she did. "What will you make in the first year?" Farhan turned, surprised, and talked for twenty minutes about storyboards. Ganga still worried about the fees. But she saw a young man choosing, not drifting, and she told him so.

passage:
Dear Imtiaz,
I'm leaving this on your desk because when we talk, I end up sounding like your Nani did with me.
When you moved back home in March, I told my friends you were "between things". I lay awake doing sums: at twenty-five I was married, working at the bank, with a baby on the way. You have changed jobs three times. I worried you were lost.
Then Rehana at work said her son's path looked just like yours, and she showed me an article saying most young people take longer to settle now. Maybe the road is simply longer than mine was.
So instead of a verdict, I have questions. What did you like in each job? What do you want the next one to have? And is there anything you need from me, other than silence at dinner?
With love and a little less worry,
Your Ammi, Ritu

qa.q: When did Imtiaz move back home?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: What was Ritu worried about as she lay awake doing sums?
qa.a: She worried Imtiaz was lost, comparing three job changes with her own life at twenty-five.

qa.q: What turning point changed Ritu's approach, and what does she do instead?
qa.a: Rehana's story and the article about longer paths made her swap a verdict for questions about what Imtiaz liked and wants next.

qa.q: How might Imtiaz feel finding questions on the desk instead of a lecture?
qa.a: Imtiaz may feel respected rather than judged, and more willing to talk than to sit in silence at dinner.

grounding: A mother worried about her twenty-five-year-old living at home and changing jobs realises paths are longer now and chooses questions over verdicts.

passage:
You asked why Vikas and I stopped fighting, Rashmi? Sit, I'll tell you.
Vikas is twenty-six. Four jobs in three years: a bank, a startup that shut, a travel company, now something with maps. And still in the room with the cricket posters. Every Sunday I'd say, "At your age your father and I had a flat and a child." Every Sunday a door would bang.
Then one night I couldn't sleep, and I actually read his CV. In every job he'd learned one thing and carried it forward. The maps job uses all of it. It wasn't drifting. It was a longer road than ours, with more turns.
Now on Sundays I ask one question instead: "What are you learning this month?" Last week he talked for an hour. He's still at home. I still worry sometimes. But I'm Kashish the mother again, not Kashish the judge.

qa.q: How many jobs has Vikas had in three years?
qa.a: Four jobs in three years.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when she read Vikas's CV?
qa.a: She felt reassured, seeing that he had learned one thing in every job and carried it forward, so it was a longer road, not drifting.

qa.q: What question did Kashish start asking, and why did it work?
qa.a: 'What are you learning this month?', which invited him to explain instead of defend himself, so he talked for an hour.

qa.q: What might Sunday dinners have felt like for Vikas before the change?
qa.a: They probably felt like a weekly verdict on his life, which is why a door banged every time.

grounding: A mother worried by her son's job changes and life at home comes to see a longer, non-linear path and starts asking questions instead of giving verdicts.

passage: I'm Yusuf, Kiran's Abbu, and I'll tell you what I saw this year, since you asked. My son is twenty-five. In twelve months he has had three jobs: the bank, a start-up, now some design studio. He still lives in his old room. At his age I was married and had a scooter loan. Every time he packed a new lunch box for a new office, I felt my chest tighten. One night I was ready to tell him he was wasting his life. Instead, I don't know why, I asked him, "What did you like in the last one?" He talked for an hour. My brother says young people now take longer. Maybe. So now I ask more than I tell.

Gopika didn't understand half of it. But she asked three more questions, and noticed she was more curious than scared.

passage: Vaibhav, you think your parents are too hard on you for moving back home? Let me tell you about my Ravi. At twenty-six he'd left two jobs in two years and was sleeping till ten in his old room. I was a school principal; I had opinions about everything. One Sunday I wrote him a long letter listing where he was going wrong. I never gave it. Because that morning I heard him on the phone, calmly helping his friend through a panic, and I thought, I don't actually know this man. So I tore up the letter and asked him to walk with me to the market. I asked what he was afraid of. He said, "Letting you down, Amma." Took him three more years to find his work. He's a good architect now. Gargi learnt late that questions open doors verdicts slam shut.

qa.a: Ravi had left two jobs in two years.

qa.q: What did Ravi say he was afraid of?
qa.a: Ravi was afraid of letting his Amma down, which suggests he felt anxious and ashamed about disappointing Gargi.

qa.q: Why was tearing up the letter a turning point in Gargi's story?
qa.a: Choosing to walk and ask questions instead of listing faults let Gargi learn what Ravi felt, rather than judging a path she didn't understand.

Four years after college, Anjali, twenty-five, was still living at home in Nashik and had changed jobs three times in two years. Her mother Jyoti lay awake worrying. At her age, Jyoti had been married, working and running a house.
One evening, watching Anjali work late on her laptop at the dining table, Jyoti nearly said, "When will you settle?" Instead she remembered what her friend had said: "Their road is longer now. Ask, don't judge."
So she brought tea and asked, "What do you like about this new job?"
Anjali looked up, surprised. "I like the team. I'm finally learning design properly."
"And moving out?"
"Maybe next year. I'm saving for it."
Jyoti nodded. Her worry didn't vanish. But she felt closer to her daughter than in months.

qa.q: How many times had Anjali changed jobs in two years?
qa.a: She had changed jobs three times.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as she watched Anjali working late?
qa.a: She felt anxious, comparing Anjali's life to her own at that age, but chose to ask rather than judge.

qa.q: Why was Jyoti's question better than 'When will you settle?'
qa.a: It invited Anjali to share what she liked and her plans, instead of issuing a verdict.

qa.q: How did Anjali react to her mother's question?
qa.a: Anjali was surprised but opened up about her team, learning design and saving to move out.

grounding: A mother worries about her adult daughter living at home and changing jobs, and chooses to ask questions instead of judging.

Kunal watched his daughter Parul, twenty-six, pack for yet another job interview in their Kolkata flat. She had moved back home after her last job ended, and at her age he'd already had a steady post and a family.
The neighbours had started asking. "Still at home? Still no fixed job?"
Kunal felt the worry sit in his stomach. But he'd been reading about how young people today take longer, switch paths, study more.
At dinner he said, "Tell me about this company. What would you do there?"
Parul looked up, surprised he wasn't lecturing. She explained about the environmental research, her eyes lighting up.
"It sounds right for you," Kunal said. "Take your time."
Parul squeezed his hand. That night he still worried. But less.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he watched Parul pack?

qa.a: Reading about how young people's paths are longer today, and asking her about the job instead of judging.

"Farhan, it's your fourth job in three years," Hansa said, drying dishes in their Bhopal kitchen.
"Ammi, please don't start."
She paused. She had rehearsed a speech about stability, about her friends' sons who were engineers with houses. But she put the towel down.
"I'm not starting. I'm asking. What went wrong at the last one?"
Farhan looked at her carefully. "Nothing went wrong. I didn't like sales. This one's in teaching. I think I'm good at it."
"Teaching," Hansa said slowly. "You did always explain things to your cousins."
"You're not angry?"
"I'm worried," she admitted. "At twenty-five I had you. But the world's different now. Just tell me when you need help."
Farhan hugged her from behind.

qa.a: His new job is in teaching.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she put the towel down?
qa.a: She felt worried about his job changes, but chose to set aside her rehearsed speech and ask instead.

qa.q: What made Hansa's response respectful?
qa.a: She asked what went wrong, admitted her worry honestly, recognised the world is different, and offered help instead of a lecture.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel about his mother's response?
qa.a: He was surprised and relieved she wasn't angry, and hugged her.

Family counsellor's note, session 2.
Mr Uday Sen came alone today. His daughter Sarika, twenty-four, has moved back home after leaving a bank job to retrain as a physiotherapist. He said, twice, 'At her age I was supporting my parents.' His hands kept tightening on his knees. He fears she is drifting. I shared, plainly, that careers now often take longer and zigzag more, and that questions may help more than verdicts. We practised: instead of 'When will you settle?', 'What's the hardest part of retraining?' He tried it aloud, stiffly, then laughed at himself. He admitted Sarika seems happier than she was at the bank, which he hadn't let himself notice. Plan: he will try one open question at dinner this week. Review in two weeks.

qa.q: What is Sarika retraining as?
qa.a: As a physiotherapist.

qa.q: What did Uday's tightening hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Uday was anxious and frustrated, fearing Sarika was drifting.

qa.q: Why is practising an open question aloud helpful for Uday?
qa.a: It turns a worried verdict into curiosity he can actually use at dinner, making a real conversation more likely.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel if her father asks 'What's the hardest part of retraining?'
qa.a: Sarika would probably feel understood and less judged, more willing to share how the retraining is going.

grounding: A counsellor notes a worried father learning to meet his adult daughter's non-linear path with questions, not verdicts.

passage:
Thursday night.
Tanvir came home at eleven again from the startup he joined in March. His fourth job since college. Twenty-five and still in his old room with the cricket posters. At the temple today Mrs Arora bragged about her son's flat in Gurgaon, and I felt that familiar tightness in my chest. What will happen to him when we're gone? Tonight I almost said it: 'When will you grow up?' But I remembered the article my niece sent me about how young people now take longer to settle, how jobs change so fast. So I sat with him while he ate and asked, 'What are you learning there?' He looked surprised. Then he talked about building an app for farmers, and I heard real pride in his voice. I'm still worried. But I'm less angry.
Rajni, keep asking.

qa.a: An app for farmers.

qa.q: What did Rajni feel when Mrs Arora bragged?
qa.a: Rajni felt a familiar tight worry in the chest, afraid for Tanvir's future.
